Well-posednesss of strongly dispersive two-dimensional surface waves Boussinesq systems

Felipe Linares Address:  IMPA
Estrada Dona Castorina 110
Rio de Janeiro 22460-320, RJ Brasil Email address: linares@impa.br , Didier Pilod Address: Instituto de Matemática, UFRJ, Caixa Postal 68530 CEP 21941-97, Rio de Janeiro, RJ Brasil Email address: didier@im.ufrj.br, pilod@impa.fr and Jean-Claude Saut Address: Laboratoire de Mathématiques, UMR 8628,
Université Paris-Sud et CNRS,
91405 Orsay, France Email address: jean-claude.saut@math.u-psud.fr
Date: April 11, 2011
Abstract.

We consider in this paper the well-posedness for the Cauchy problem associated to two-dimensional dispersive systems of Boussinesq type which model weakly nonlinear long wave surface waves. We emphasize the case of the strongly dispersive ones with focus on the “KdV-KdV” system which possesses the strongest dispersive properties and which is a vector two-dimensional extension of the classical KdV equation.

1. Introduction

1.1. General Setting

In general, nonlinear dispersive equations and systems are not derived from first principles. They are obtained as asymptotic models (normal forms) when some small parameter tends to zero, of more general systems, under a suitable scaling. There are supposed to describe the dynamics under suitable scaling conditions. We will study in this article small amplitude, long wave models which have the general form

(1) Ut+A​U+ϵ​F​(U,∇U)+ϵ​L​U=0.U_{t}+AU+\epsilon F(U,\nabla U)+\epsilon LU=0.

Here ϵ\epsilon is a “small” parameter which takes into account the nonlinear and dispersive effects, which are assumed of the same order. U=U⁡(x,t)U=U(x,t) is a vector in ℝn+1{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}, n=1,2n=1,2 and x∈ℝn,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, t>0.t>0. The order zero part Ut+A​UU_{t}+AU is just the linear wave equation, while the third and fourth terms in (1) represents the nonlinear and dispersive effects. The right-hand side of (1) should in fact be O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}).

A typical example is that of the abcd Boussinesq systems for long, small amplitude gravity surface water waves introduced in [6], [5]

(2) {ηt+∇⋅𝐯+ϵ[∇⋅(η𝐯)+a∇⋅Δ𝐯−bΔηt]=0𝐯t+∇η+ϵ[12∇|𝐯|2+c∇Δη−dΔ𝐯t]=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+\nabla\cdot{\bf v}+\epsilon[\nabla\cdot(\eta{\bf v})+a\nabla\cdot\Delta{\bf v}-b\Delta\eta_{t}]=0\\ {\bf v}_{t}+\nabla\eta+\epsilon[\frac{1}{2}\nabla|{\bf v}|^{2}+c\nabla\Delta\eta-d\Delta{\bf v}_{t}]=0.\par\end{array}\right.

Here, η\eta is the deviation of the free surface from its rest state and 𝐯{\bf v} is an O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}) approximation of the horizontal velocity taken at a certain depth (see [6], [5]). The constants a,b,c,da,b,c,d are modeling parameters subject to the constraint a+b+c+d=13.a+b+c+d=\frac{1}{3}. Those three degrees of freedom arise from the choice of the height at which the velocity is taken and from a double use of the BBM trick.

The small parameter ϵ\epsilon is defined by

ϵ=a/h∼(h/λ)2,\epsilon=a/h\sim(h/\lambda)^{2},

where hh denotes the mean depth of the fluid, aa a typical amplitude of the wave and λ\lambda a typical horizontal wavelength.

Those systems are approximations of the full water wave system in the so-called Boussinesq regime (see [6], [5]). They degenerate into the KdV (or BBM) equation in the one-dimensional case, for waves traveling in one direction. They also appear as models for internal waves, in an appropriate regime (see [9], [11]). When surface tension effects are taken into account, the coefficient cc should be changed into c−τc-\tau where τ≥0\tau\geq 0 is the surface tension parameter (see [14]). Throughout the paper we will consider only the case of purely gravity waves, that is τ=0.\tau=0.

Of course restrictions are to be imposed on a,b,c,da,b,c,d in order that the linear part of (2) be well-posed. It was established in [7] that, when n=1n=1, all the linearly well-posed systems are locally nonlinearly well-posed. As for the two-dimensional case (n=2n=2), it has been proved in [15] that in the generic case where b>0,d>0b>0,\;d>0 one has well-posedness on time scales of order O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}) for data in the Sobolev space H1H^{1}. The local well-posedness in other cases (but not in the strongly dispersive “KdV-KdV” case) was proved in [13], but the question of the dependence of the time existence with respect to ϵ\epsilon was not addressed there.

One of the goals of the present paper is to complete the local well-posedness theory for a,b,c,da,b,c,d systems in two dimensions, with focus on the size of the lifespan of the solutions with respect to ϵ\epsilon.

An interesting fact (already noticed in [6]) from the PDE view point is that, though the a,b,c,da,b,c,d systems describe the same wave propagation phenomenon, their dispersive properties are quite different. We will precise the dispersion matrix in Section 2. After diagonalization, one is led to two-dimensional systems with strong dispersion (of KdV or Schrödinger type) or with weak dispersion (for instance of BBM type). One also obtains a system which can be viewed as a dispersive perturbation of the two-dimensional Saint-Venant (shallow-water) system, generalizing the one-dimensional system studied by Amick [2] and Schonbek [30].

On the other hand, the solutions of the Cauchy problem associated to (2) should exist on time scales of order O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) in order to prove that the asymptotic system is a good approximation of the water wave system [1]. In fact, the solutions of (2) cease to be relevant as approximations of those of the original system on time scales larger than O⁡(1ϵ2).O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}).

It is worth noticing that it is unlikely that all the abcd systems would have global solutions. In fact they are shown to be Hamiltonian (and thus possess a formally conserved energy) only when b=db=d (see [6]). This can be used in the one-dimensional case to obtain the global well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for a few of the systems see [7] but this situation is exceptional and moreover does not apply to the two-dimensional case where the Hamiltonian does not control any Sobolev type norm.

This situation is in strong contrast with one-directional models such as the Korteweg- de Vries (KdV) or Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (BBM) equations or with quasi one-directional models such as the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation where global a priori bounds are available (possibly at low degree of regularity), which allows to prove the global well-posedness of the Cauchy problem.

As far as we know the problem of solving any of the systems (2) on time intervals of order O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) has been completely open until very recently, except for some one-dimensional ones which have global solutions (under some restrictions on the initial data).

In [5] Bona , Colin and Lannes obtained an order O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) existence interval for a fully symmetric class of systems, in one and two dimensions. Those systems have a skew-adjoint linear part (a=ca=c) and are obtained from (2) via the nonlinear change of variables 𝐯~=𝐯⁡(1+ϵ2​η)\tilde{{\bf v}}={\bf v}(1+\frac{\epsilon}{2}\eta) which does not affect the linear part (modulo higher order terms in ϵ\epsilon) and which symmetrizes the nonlinear part. Neglecting the higher order terms in ϵ\epsilon, one obtain skew-adjoint perturbations of symmetric quasilinear hyperbolic systems and the classical theory of this kind of systems provides the O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) existence time. This method does not use the dispersive part of the systems and of course does not solve the long time existence problem for the abcd systems.

In [27] an approach based on a Nash-Moser theorem is developed to prove well-posedness results for the 2D- Boussinesq systems 11 1 This approach gives also similar results in the one dimensional case. on time intervals of order 1/ϵ1/\epsilon. In [27] the generic case, that is when b>0,d>0,a<0,c<0b>0,d>0,a<0,c<0 and the BBM/BBM case, that is when b>0,d>0,a=c=0b>0,d>0,a=c=0 are emphasized but the approach could very likely be applied to other cases . This method does not use the dispersive part of the systems and a high regularity level in required on the initial data, with loss of regularity on the solution.

The aim of the present paper is to prove the well-posedness for the most dispersive of the two-dimensional Boussinesq systems (2) on time scales of order ϵ−1/2,\epsilon^{-1/2}, using the dispersive properties of the systems. This allows to consider relatively rough initial data. We will in particular obtain uniformly bounded in ϵ\epsilon solutions on time scales of order T/ϵT/\sqrt{\epsilon} in suitable Sobolev spaces, achieving the rigorous justification of those models on the corresponding time scales (see [1]). Note however that we are not able in our functional setting to reach the optimal time scales O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}).

The heart of the paper concerns the most dispersive Boussinesq system (the KdV-KdV system) where a=c=1/6,b=d=0a=c=1/6,b=d=0 which is an interesting two-dimensional extension of the Korteweg-de Vries equation 22 2 There are relatively few physically relevant systems of this form. for which the local well-posedness is not a simple matter. Our method deeply lies on dispersive estimates for the underlying linear problem. In particular we establish new Strichartz and maximal function estimates.

For the other cases (which are less dispersive), at least when d>0,d>0, 33 3 When d=0d=0 it is unclear whether the local well-posedness can be obtained by elementary energy methods in the 2​D2D case without imposing the irrotationality of the velocity. the proofs are the extension to the two-dimensional case of those given by energy estimates in [7] for the one-dimensional case, keeping track of the ϵ\epsilon’s but we do not pursue this issue here. We will focus instead on the order 22 Boussinesq systems which can be written as systems of nonlinear nonlocal Schrödinger type equations coupled by the nonlinear terms. Some of those cases have been studied in [13] but the ϵ\epsilon dependence of the existence time interval was not addressed here and the difficulty linked to the case d=0d=0 was underestimated.

1.2. Organization of the paper

The paper is organized as follows.

Section 2 recall briefly some useful facts on the Boussinesq systems.

In Section 3 we will consider the KdV-KdV Boussinesq system, and establish the well-posedness in the two-dimensional case, on time intervals of order ϵ−1/2,\epsilon^{-1/2}, after establishing various dispersive estimates for the solutions of the linear part.

In Section 4, we consider the well-posedness of the remaining strongly dispersive cases ( Schrödinger type) to prove that there are also well-posed on time intervals of order ϵ−1/2.\epsilon^{-1/2}. There are essentially two cases, depending whether bb or dd vanishes.

2. Classification of Boussinesq systems

The Boussinesq systems can be conveniently classified according to the linearization at the null solutions which display their dispersive properties [7]. More precisely, the dispersion matrix writes in Fourier variables,

A^​(ξ1,ξ2)=i​(0ξ1​(1−ϵ​a​|ξ|2)OPEN1+ϵ​b​|ξ|2)ξ2​(1−ϵ​a​|ξ2|2)OPEN1+ϵ​b​|ξ|2)ξ1​(1−ϵ​c​|ξ|2CLOSEOPEN1+ϵ​d​|ξ|2)00ξ2​(1−ϵ​c​|ξ|2CLOSEOPEN1+ϵ​d​|ξ|2)00).\widehat{A}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=i\begin{pmatrix}0&\frac{\xi_{1}(1-\epsilon a|\xi|^{2})}{1+\epsilon b|\xi|^{2})}&\frac{\xi_{2}(1-\epsilon a|\xi^{2}|^{2})}{1+\epsilon b|\xi|^{2})}\\ \frac{\xi_{1}(1-\epsilon c|\xi|^{2}}{1+\epsilon d|\xi|^{2})}&0&0\\ \\ \frac{\xi_{2}(1-\epsilon c|\xi|^{2}}{1+\epsilon d|\xi|^{2})}&0&0\end{pmatrix}.

The corresponding non zero eigenvalues are

λ±=±i​|ξ|​((1−ϵ​a​|ξ|2)​(1−ϵ​c​|ξ|2)(1+ϵ​d​|ξ|2)​(1+ϵ​b​|ξ|2))12.\lambda_{\pm}=\pm i|\xi|\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon a|\xi|^{2})(1-\epsilon c|\xi|^{2})}{(1+\epsilon d|\xi|^{2})(1+\epsilon b|\xi|^{2})}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

Recall [6] that the well-posedness of the linearized Boussinesq system requires that b≥0,d≥0b\geq 0,\;d\geq 0 and a≤0,c≤0,a\leq 0,\;c\leq 0, (or OPENa=c)a=c).

The order of λ±\lambda_{\pm} determine the strength of the dispersion in the Boussinesq systems, the more dispersive one corresponding to b=d=0,b=d=0, the so called KdV-KdV case which will be studied in details in the next section.

By “weakly dispersive” Boussinesq systems, we mean the case where b>0b>0 and d>0d>0, so that λ±\lambda_{\pm} have order 1, 0​or−1.1,\;0\;\text{or}\;-1.

This situation has been studied in [15] where it is established for instance in the generic case with a<0a<0 and c<0c<0 that the Cauchy problem is well-posed in C​([0,Tϵ],H1​(ℝ2))2C([0,T_{\epsilon}];H^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}))^{2} where TϵT_{\epsilon} is of order O⁡(1ϵβ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{\beta}}) for any β<12\beta<\frac{1}{2}.

As already mentioned, existence on time intervals of order O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) has been established for weakly dispersive Boussinesq systems when the initial data are smooth (and with a loss of derivatives) in [27].

3. The KdV-KdV Boussinesq system

We are interested in the following dispersive system

(3) {∂tη+div​v+ϵ​div​(η​v)+ϵ​div​Δ​v=0∂tv+∇η+ϵ12∇(|v|2)+ϵ∇Δη=0,(x1,x2)∈ℝ2,t∈ℝ,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\eta+\text{div}\,\textbf{v}+\epsilon\text{div}\,(\eta\textbf{v})+\epsilon\text{div}\,\Delta\textbf{v}=0\\ \partial_{t}\textbf{v}+\nabla\eta+\epsilon\frac{1}{2}\nabla(|\textbf{v}|^{2})+\epsilon\nabla\Delta\eta=0\end{array}\right.,\quad(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\ t\in\mathbb{R},

which corresponds to the case where b=d=0b=d=0 and a=c=16.a=c=\frac{1}{6}. We have scaled aa and cc to the value 11. This system might not be the best one as modeling and numerical purposes are concerned (in particular the cubic dispersion terms induce serious numerical difficulties). Nevertheless (3) is a mathematically interesting system since it can be written as a nonlocal two-dimensional version of a KdV -type system. Previous results concerned the one-dimensional version:

(4) {ηt+vx+ϵ​(η​v)x+ϵ​vx​x​x=0vt+ηx+ϵ2​(v2)x+ϵ​ηx​x​x=0,x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+v_{x}+\epsilon(\eta v)_{x}+\epsilon v_{xxx}=0\\ v_{t}+\eta_{x}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}(v^{2})_{x}+\epsilon\eta_{xxx}=0\end{array}\right.,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\ t\in\mathbb{R}.

Actually, as noticed in [7], the change of variable η=u+w,v=u−w\eta=u+w,\;v=u-w reduces (4) to the following system:

(5) {ut+ux+ϵ​ux​x​x+ϵ⁡[2​u​ux+(u​w)x]=0wt−wx−ϵ​wx​x​x+ϵ⁡[−2​w​wx+(u​w)x]=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}+u_{x}+\epsilon u_{xxx}+\epsilon[2uu_{x}+(uw)_{x}]=0\\ w_{t}-w_{x}-\epsilon w_{xxx}+\epsilon[-2ww_{x}+(uw)_{x}]=0\end{array}\right.,

which is a system of KdV type with uncoupled (diagonal) linear part. Thus (see [7]) the Cauchy problem is easily seen to be locally well-posed for initial data in Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ),H^{s}({\mathbb{R}})\times H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}), s>34s>\frac{3}{4} by the results in [20], [21]. On the other hand, as noticed in [29] Appendix A in a slightly different context, a minor modification of Bourgain’s method as used in [23] allows to solve the Cauchy problem for (5) for data in Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}({\mathbb{R}})\times H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}) with s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}. We refer to [8] for details. It is worth noticing that in [8] the question of the dependence of the existence time with respect to ϵ\epsilon is not considered.

Coming back to the two-dimensional system, we will establish that the Cauchy problem is locally well-posed for data in Hs​(ℝ2)×Hs​(ℝ2)2H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\times H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})^{2} where s>32s>\frac{3}{2}.

Theorem 1.

Let s>32s>\frac{3}{2} and 0<ϵ≤10<\epsilon\leq 1 be fixed. Then for any (η0,v0)∈Hs​(ℝ2)×Hs​(ℝ2)2(\eta_{0},\textbf{v}_{0})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})^{2} with curl v0=0\mbox{{curl }}\textbf{v}_{0}=0, there exist a positive time T=T⁡(‖(η0,v0)‖Hs×(Hs)2)T=T(\|(\eta_{0},\textbf{v}_{0})\|_{H^{s}\times(H^{s})^{2}}), a space YTϵsY^{s}_{T_{\epsilon}} such that

(6) YTϵs↪C⁡([0,Tϵ],Hs​(ℝ2)×Hs​(ℝ2)2),Y^{s}_{T_{\epsilon}}\hookrightarrow C\big([0,T_{\epsilon}]\ ;\ H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})^{2}\big),

and a unique solution (η,v)(\eta,\textbf{v}) to (3) in YTϵsY^{s}_{T_{\epsilon}} satisfying (η,v)|t=0=(η0,v0)(\eta,\textbf{v})_{|_{t=0}}=(\eta_{0},\textbf{v}_{0}), where Tϵ=T​ϵ−12T_{\epsilon}=T\epsilon^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

Moreover, for any T′∈(0,Tϵ)T^{\prime}\in(0,T_{\epsilon}), there exists a neighborhood Ωs\Omega^{s} of (η0,v0)(\eta_{0},\textbf{v}_{0}) in Hs​(ℝ2)×Hs​(ℝ2)2H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})^{2} such that the flow map associated to (3) is smooth from Ωs\Omega^{s} into YT′sY^{s}_{T^{\prime}}.

Remark 1.

Our proof applies as well with minor modifications to Boussinesq systems with b=d=0b=d=0 and a<0,a<0, c<0c<0. While this case is excluded for systems modeling purely gravity waves, it may happen for capillary-gravity waves when the surface tension parameter τ\tau is large enough.

Remark 2.

It transpires from the proof of Theorem 1 that the solution is uniformly bounded (with respect to ϵ\epsilon) in the corresponding spaces on a time interval [0,Tϵ][0,\frac{T}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}].

The strategy is first to diagonalize the linear part of (3). We thus reduce the original system to a nonlocal one. In particular, the nonlinear part involves order zero pseudo-differential operators (in fact Riesz transforms). We then solve the underlying Duhamel integral formulation by a fixed point argument in a ball of a Banach space constructed from the various dispersive estimates satisfied by the linear part. Note that here, we are able to compute the dependence on ϵ\epsilon of the constants appearing in the linear estimates. This allows us to obtain an existence result in a time interval [0,T][0,T] depending on ϵ\epsilon, in our case T∼ϵ−12T\sim\epsilon^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

We will thus proceed as follows. We first derive the Hamiltonian formulation of (3). We then perform the diagonalization and state the dispersive estimates which are to be used in the fixed point argument. The maximal function and Strichartz estimates seem to be new. Finally, we solve the new system (10) which is equivalent to (3), assuming curl ​𝐯0=0\mbox{{curl }}{\bf v}_{0}=0.

3.1. Hamiltonian structure

The system (3) can be rewritten on the form

(7) ∂tu+Aϵ​u+ϵ​𝒩​(u)=0,\partial_{t}\textbf{u}+A_{\epsilon}\textbf{u}+\epsilon\mathcal{N}(\textbf{u})=0,

where

3.2.4. Strichartz estimates

Strichartz estimates for unitary groups of the form ei​t​ϕ​(D)e^{it\phi(D)} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, were derived in the case where ϕ\phi is an elliptic polynomial by Kenig, Ponce and Vega [19] and in the case where ϕ\phi is a general polynomial in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} by Ben-Artzi, Koch and Saut [3]. When the phase function ϕ\phi is a radial (nonhomogeneous) function and its derivative does not vanish, some techniques were recently developed by Cho and Ozawa [12] and Guo, Peng and Wang [16].

In the sequel, we will use the techniques developed in [16], based on the ones used in [19] and on the representation of the Fourier transform of a radial function in terms of the Bessel function (see formula (21)), to prove Strichartz estimates associated to the unitary groups Uϵ±U^{\pm}_{\epsilon} defined in (12). 4. Other strongly dispersive Boussinesq systems

Other two-dimensional Boussinesq systems can be classified according to the order of the eigenvalues of the dispersion matrix (see Introduction). As we already mentioned, when b,d>0b,d>0, the well-posedness on time scales of order 1/ϵ1/{\sqrt{\epsilon}} has been established in [15] for initial data in low order Sobolev spaces and on time interval of order 1/ϵ1/{\epsilon} in [27] for smooth initial data (with loss of derivatives). We thus restrict ourselves to the case where at least one of the coefficients bb or dd vanishes, emphasizing the strongest dispersive case corresponding to eigenvalues of order 22 (the so-called “Schrödinger” type systems) where a<0a<0 and c<0.c<0.

The local well posedness for some of those systems has been established in the two-dimensional case by Cung The Anh [13], but without looking for the dependence of the existence time with respect to ϵ\epsilon. Note however that the proof given in [13] for the case where d=0d=0 (Theorem 3.5) does not seem to be correct.

We will complete the analysis, in particular by checking the ϵ\epsilon dependence. It turns out that when d>0,d>0, one can establish the local well-posedness of Boussinesq “Schrödinger” type systems on time intervals of order 1/ϵ1/{\sqrt{\epsilon}} by elementary energy methods, in relatively low order Sobolev spaces.

We first state a useful lemma.

4.1. Schrödinger type Boussinesq systems when d>0d>0

As already mentioned, attention is focused here in systems where the eigenvalues λ±​(ξ)\lambda_{\pm}(\xi) are of order 22. Because of the constraint on a,b,c,da,b,c,d the only possibilities are a<0,a<0, c<0,c<0, b=0b=0, d>0d>0 or a<0,a<0, c<0,c<0, b>0,b>0, d=0d=0. 44 4 When surface tension is large enough so that τ>1/3\tau>1/3, we have the admissible system a=b=d=0,c=τ−1/3a=b=d=0,\;c=\tau-1/3 but we will note consider it here. We will study here the first case and thus consider the systems

(74) {ηt+∇⋅𝐯+ϵ[∇⋅(η𝐯)+a∇⋅Δ𝐯]=0𝐯t+∇η+ϵ[12∇|𝐯|2+c∇Δη−dΔ𝐯t]=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+\nabla\cdot{\bf v}+\epsilon[\nabla\cdot(\eta{\bf v})+a\nabla\cdot\Delta{\bf v}]=0\\ {\bf v}_{t}+\nabla\eta+\epsilon[\frac{1}{2}\nabla|{\bf v}|^{2}+c\nabla\Delta\eta-d\Delta{\bf v}_{t}]=0,\end{array}\right.

where a<0,a<0, c<0,c<0, d>0.d>0.

Those systems are called in [7] “Benjamin-Ono type systems” since the dispersion matrix has, in the one-dimensional case and when ϵ=1\epsilon=1, eigenvalues equal to ±((a​cd)12​k​|k|+r⁡(k))\pm((\frac{ac}{d})^{\frac{1}{2}}k|k|+r(k)) where r⁡(k)r(k) is 0​(1|k|)0(\frac{1}{|k|}) as k→∞.k\to\infty.

In the two-dimensional case, the dispersion matrix in Fourier variables reads

A^​(ξ1,ξ2)=i​(0ξ1​(1−ϵ​a​|ξ|2)ξ2​(1−ϵ​a​|ξ|2)ξ1​(1−ϵ​c​|ξ|2)1+ϵ​d​|ξ|200ξ2​(1−ϵ​c​|ξ|2)1+ϵ​d​|ξ|200).\widehat{A}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=i\begin{pmatrix}0&\xi_{1}(1-\epsilon a|\xi|^{2})&\xi_{2}(1-\epsilon a|\xi|^{2})\\ \frac{\xi_{1}(1-\epsilon c|\xi|^{2})}{1+\epsilon d|\xi|^{2}}&0&0\\ \\ \frac{\xi_{2}(1-\epsilon c|\xi|^{2})}{1+\epsilon d|\xi|^{2}}&0&0\end{pmatrix}.

The corresponding nonzero eigenvalues are

λ±=±|ξ|​((1−ϵ​a​|ξ|2)​(1−ϵ​c​|ξ|2)1+ϵ​d​|ξ|2)12.\lambda_{\pm}=\pm|\xi|\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon a|\xi|^{2})(1-\epsilon c|\xi|^{2})}{1+\epsilon d|\xi|^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

For ϵ\epsilon fixed, λ±\lambda_{\pm} are equivalent as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty to ±ϵ​(a​cd)12​|ξ|2,\pm\epsilon\left(\frac{ac}{d}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}|\xi|^{2}, which explains the terminology “Schrödinger type” Boussinesq systems.

After diagonalization of the linear part, (74) can thus be written as a (nonlinearly coupled) system of two Schrödinger type nonlocal equations involving derivatives of the unknowns, and we might think of solving the Cauchy problem by applying the general results of [24]. We will refrain to do that here because an elementary energy method on the original formulation (74), which is the extension to the two-dimensional case of the corresponding one-dimensional result in [7] applies when d>0,d>0, and when d=0d=0 for curlfree velocities.

Then, for every (η0,𝐯0)∈Hs+2​(ℝ2)×Hs+1​(ℝ2)2(\eta_{0},{\bf v}_{0})\in H^{s+2}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\times H^{s+1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})^{2} with curl ​𝐯0=0\mbox{{curl }}{\bf v}_{0}=0 there exist T=T⁡(‖η0‖Hs+2,‖𝐯0‖Hs+1)T=T(||\eta_{0}||_{H^{s+2}},||{\bf v}_{0}||_{H^{s+1}}) and a unique solution

(η,𝐯)∈C⁡([0,Tϵ],Hs+2​(ℝ2))×C⁡([0,Tϵ],Hs+1​(ℝ2)2),(\eta,{\bf v})\in C([0,T_{\epsilon}];H^{s+2}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}))\times C([0,T_{\epsilon}];H^{s+1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})^{2}),

where Tϵ=Tϵ−1/2T_{\epsilon}=T\epsilon^{-1/2} of (74) with initial data (η0,𝐯0)(\eta_{0},{\bf v}_{0}) which is uniformly bounded on [0,Tϵ].[0,T_{\epsilon}].

The proof of Theorem 7 is very similar to that of Theorem 6 and we only sketch it. We will use the following estimate.

Lemma 7.

Let s>2s>2 and 𝐯∈Hs​(ℝ2){\bf v}\in H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) such that curl ​𝐯=0.\mbox{{curl }}{\bf v}=0. Then

|∫ℝ2Λs∇|𝐯|2⋅Λs𝐯|≤C∥𝐯∥3Hs.\Big|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\Lambda^{s}\nabla|{\bf v}|^{2}\cdot\Lambda^{s}{\bf v}\Big|\leq C\|{\bf v}\|^{3}_{H^{s}}.
Proof.

Let 𝐯=(v1,v2)T.{\bf v}=(v_{1},v_{2})^{T}. Then ∂x1v2=∂x2v1\partial_{x_{1}}v_{2}=\partial_{x_{2}}v_{1} and

12∇|𝐯|2=(v1∂x1v1+v2∂x2v1,v1∂x1v2+v2∂x2v2)T.\frac{1}{2}\nabla|{\bf v}|^{2}=(v_{1}\partial_{x_{1}}v_{1}+v_{2}\partial_{x_{2}}v_{1},v_{1}\partial_{x_{1}}v_{2}+v_{2}\partial_{x_{2}}v_{2})^{T}.

The estimate then follows immediately from integration by parts, the Kato-Ponce commutator lemma and the embedding Hs−1​(ℝ2)↪L∞​(ℝ2).H^{s-1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}). ∎

Proof of Theorem 7.

(i) Uniqueness. Again we consider ϵ=1\epsilon=1. Let (η1,𝐯1),(\eta_{1},{\bf v}_{1}), (η2,𝐯2)(\eta_{2},{\bf v}_{2}) two solutions and let N=η1−η2,N=\eta_{1}-\eta_{2}, 𝐕=𝐯1−𝐯2.{\bf V}={\bf v}_{1}-{\bf v}_{2}. We have therefore

(85) {Nt+∇⋅𝐕+ϵ[∇⋅(N𝐯1+η2𝐕)+a∇⋅Δ𝐕−bΔNt]=0𝐕t+∇N+ϵ[12∇(𝐕⋅(𝐯1+𝐯2))+c∇ΔN]=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}N_{t}+\nabla\cdot{\bf V}+\epsilon[\nabla\cdot(N{\bf v}_{1}+\eta_{2}{\bf V})+a\nabla\cdot\Delta{\bf V}-b\Delta N_{t}]=0\\ {\bf V}_{t}+\nabla N+\epsilon[\frac{1}{2}\nabla({\bf V}\cdot({\bf v}_{1}+{\bf v}_{2}))+c\nabla\Delta N]=0.\end{array}\right.

We multiply the first equation by −c​N-cN, take scalar product of the second one by −a​𝐕-a{\bf V}, integrate and sum. One obtains after integrations by parts

12​dd​t∫ℝ2[|c|​N2+|a|​|𝐕|2+|c|​b​|∇N|2]≤C⁡(‖𝐯1‖L∞,‖η2‖L∞,‖∇𝐯1‖L∞,‖∇𝐯2‖L∞)​[‖N‖L22+‖∇N‖L22+‖𝐕‖L22],\begin{split}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}&\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}[|c|N^{2}+|a||{\bf V}|^{2}+|c|b|\nabla N|^{2}]\\ &\leq C(\|{\bf v}_{1}\|_{L^{\infty}},\|\eta_{2}\|_{L^{\infty}},\|\nabla{\bf v}_{1}\|_{L^{\infty}},\|\nabla{\bf v}_{2}\|_{L^{\infty}})[\|N\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\nabla N\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|{\bf V}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}],\end{split}

and the result follows from Gronwall’s lemma.

(ii) Existence. We just indicate how to obtain the energy estimates in the case a=ca=c. We apply the operator Λs\Lambda^{s} to both equations of (74), multiply the first one by Λs​η\Lambda^{s}\eta, take the scalar product of the second one by Λs​𝐯\Lambda^{s}{\bf v}, integrate and sum to get using Kato-Ponce Lemma and Lemma 7

(86) dd​t[∥Λsη∥L22+∥Λs𝐯∥L22+ϵb∥∇Λsη∥L22]≤Cϵ|∫ℝ2Λs∇⋅(η𝐯)Λsη+Λs∇|𝐯|2⋅Λs𝐯|≤C​ϵ​(‖∇𝐯‖L∞​‖Λs​η‖L22+‖𝐯‖Hs3),\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}[\|\Lambda^{s}\eta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}&+\|\Lambda^{s}{\bf v}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\epsilon b\|\nabla\Lambda^{s}\eta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}]\\ &\leq C\epsilon\Big|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\Lambda^{s}\nabla\cdot(\eta{\bf v})\Lambda^{s}\eta+\Lambda^{s}\nabla|{\bf v}|^{2}\cdot\Lambda^{s}{\bf v}\Big|\\ &\leq C\epsilon\big(\|\nabla{\bf v}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\Lambda^{s}\eta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|{\bf v}\|^{3}_{H^{s}}\big),\end{split}

from which one obtain the expected a priori uniform estimate on a time interval [0,T/ϵ].[0,T/\sqrt{\epsilon}].

When a≠ca\neq c one has to modify the proof as in Theorem 6. ∎

5. Final comments

To keep this paper short and to maintain a certain unity, we have refrain here to consider the other Boussinesq systems, which have eigenvalues λ±\lambda_{\pm} of order 11 or less. For instance the cases a=c=b=0,a=c=b=0, d=1/3d=1/3 or a=c=d=0,a=c=d=0, b=1/3b=1/3 are version of Boussinesq original system. The former case has been studied in the one-dimensional case by Schonbek [30] and Amick [2] who obtained global well-posedness by viewing the system as a (dispersive) perturbation of the Saint-Venant (shallow-water) hyperbolic system.

In both cases, no results seem to be available in two-dimensions.
